utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, we can start with the next witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I used the time to deal with a matter related to the testimony of Emir Turkusic. The Chamber would like to put on the record that the Defence has complied with the Chamber's instructions on transcript page 18196 regarding D351. The Prosecution indicated in an informal communication which was dated the 28th of October of this year, that the revised translation for P2043 has been received and that it will be uploaded and replaced soon. The Chamber instructs the Prosecution to inform the Chamber on the record once this has been done. The Chamber further understands that the parties are in possession of both the 82- and the 120-millimetre rule-books and considers this matter to be resolved. I have another matter in relation to Witness Turkusic, but I'll leave that for a later moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rechner, I presume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Rechner, you'll first be examined by Ms. Bibles. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Bibles, as you most likely know already, is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, Patrick Anthony Rechner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us your current rank in the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the witness statement, 65 ter 30416, be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Once the document appears, I'll ask if you recognise it. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And is this your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And have you signed this -- or whose signature is on this first page?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And did you initial every page in this statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll advise you that the witness requested a copy of his statement for his use during his testimony. We have provided a clean copy of that document for him, and he is referring to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any need to consult your statement, please inform the Chamber that you need to consult it before doing so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this amalgamated statement prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are there any changes or corrections that you would make to this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If you were asked about the substance of these matters today, would you give the same answers that are contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I -- yes, in substance, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Having taken the solemn oath, do you affirm that the information in this document is accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 30416.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30416 receives number P2554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2554 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also tender the table of concordance that aligns the exhibit numbers in the statement with the exhibit numbers in this case. That is 65 ter 30164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30164 receives number P2555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2525 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I correct myself. P2555 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may read a brief summary of the witness's written testimony, the purposes of which has been explained to the witness, and I believe we've provided copies to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Patrick Rechner was a Canadian United Nations Military Observer who was posted to Pale on 31 December 1994. He worked as a liaison between the parties, and the parties and UNPROFOR. In this capacity he communicated with the primary office of the Bosnian Serb leadership and military. He also assisted in humanitarian efforts for the community, including, securing medications for the local hospital. Mr. Rechner describes that given his background, he was humiliated and betrayed when he was taken hostage on 26 May 1995 and, along with other United Nations Military Observers, was threatened with death and used as a human shield. The witness was released on 18 June 1995. And this concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions to the witness, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's direct attention to the events described in your statement in paragraphs 36, 39. Have you had an opportunity to watch a video that captures some of the sequence of events described here on film?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you depicted in this video?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we turn to play the video, I will advise the Trial Chamber and the booth that there is a small amount of discussion captured on these videos. There is no narration. Transcripts of the intelligible sections have been provided to the booths. To assist in the process of playing these videos, we will play this approximate five-minute video in four sections. We would rely on the transcript sections only in the first and the last segments. Because the time code on the transcripts were based on the original video, I will provide some assistance in indicating on the transcripts which sections will be played prior to actually playing those. With that in mind, Your Honours, I'd ask Ms. Stewart to play 65 ter 22648A from 0 to 1 minute, 24 seconds. On the transcript's time code it would reflect the section from 38:16 to 39:41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just get clarification, Ms. Bibles. Where is the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The original video was seized by NATO, I believe, in 2009, and it was a compilation of home-type videos. Though it has -- the original video is quite long and has a lengthy segments, we would only be introducing this five-minute segment from that original video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do we know who transcribed this copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just to clarify, this segment was transcribed in-house with OTP by language assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- has the Defence any problems with the transcription as we have it now? Because then we might be able to play it only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We don't. We have already stated as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it can be played once and the basis for the translation could be the transcription. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "What's he saying? "I didn't understand them. "Stay here with them. Fuck it. They should all be... "You will die if they bomb. You will die for the good of NATO. "This is 7-9, over. 7-9. We have been instructed to advise you that..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 39, you describe that footage is recorded by a lieutenant-colonel in the Bosnian Serb army. Is this a portion of the video that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the first section of the footage, which depicts three men handcuffed to each other and to a door. Could you please tell us who the men are?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. As you're looking at the video, the person on the left is myself; in the centre, is the Czech officer in my military observer team, at the time Captain Oldrich, Oli, Zidlik; and then on the right is, at the time, Captain Pavel Teterevsky from Russia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What is the location of that portion of the footage?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The first images that you saw where we were handcuffed through the door of our UN military observer vehicle, that was just inside a large military facility within which a few kilometres away were located the targets of the actual bombing. And at that time, the bombing was still in progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you also in the video segment that we saw within a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe for us what, if anything, you did during that segment of the video.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That segment depicts us driving from that initial location where we were handcuffed through the door of the vehicle, driving towards the actual ammunition bunkers that were being bombed at the time. And that segment occurred just after we had received over our radio system the all clear from our UNMO headquarters that they had received information that the air-strikes had been called off, so we were just driving towards those targets at that time. We didn't know exactly what was going on, what their intentions were for us. But the clip that you saw, I was asked to contact my headquarters and relay the comment made by this Serb lieutenant-colonel who was the video man saying that if any more bombing occurred, and I changed the words slightly to say that, We've been instructed to inform you that we are to die for the sake of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I'd ask Ms. Stewart to play the segment from 1 minute 24 to 3 minutes in three sections.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Here it is. They're still shooting up there. "Wait here. Oh, my dear Russian. Are you Russian? "Call Kozirev. He can save you. To hell with him. "Not the hands. "Find a wire. "There will be a lot of UNPROFOR in this circle this evening, just to let you know."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The last segment here, can you tell us who is depicted in the image?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: This image that's in front of me, that's myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us the -- the structures that surround you at that point.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: There were four hardened ammunition bunkers located next to each other side by side just across that dirt road that you can see in front of me. Two of them had been destroyed in that morning's bombing and two were still unaffected, so I was handcuffed, as you can see in this image, to a lightening [Realtime transcript read in error "whitening"] rod directly in front of one of those bunker that had not been damaged yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the witness said the image in front of me, the still at 3 minutes, 2 seconds, 2 and a half seconds was shown. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us which other United Nations Military Observers were depicted in the video segment that we've just watched?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: They were the same ones that I mentioned a few minutes ago. These are the members of my team. The other two were -- that is, the ones I mentioned are Captain Oli Zidlik from the Czech Republic and Captain Pavel Teterevsky from Russia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At some point in time while you were handcuffed in this location, were other United Nations individuals brought to this location?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, approximately one and a half or two hours later, we saw members of another UN Military Observer team that was also based in Pale that were known by their radio call-sign Sierra Echo 1, and there were five individuals in that team that we saw in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a correction. At page 9, line 17, you say, "So I was handcuffed, as you can see in this image, to a whitening rod." That is how you were transcribed as having said. Did you say "whitening rod"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Lightening rod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lightening rod. I thought that's what you said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd now ask Ms. Stewart to play from 3 minutes and 2 seconds to 3 minutes and 38 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let's take a photo. Stand over there. "Pale innocent civilians were injured and killed... this is an act of... NATO strikes. "Tell him that Milos got injured." 25

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know where the bridge that's depicted in this segment is located?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's in the town of Pale, a few hundred metres from the actual location of our accommodation and office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know who the two men are who are depicted sitting down or kneeling right next to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Those are two members, that is, two UNMOs from the Sierra Echo 1 team, which is, as I mentioned, the other observer team that was based in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd now ask Ms. Stewart to play the segment from -- this play -- this location at 3 minutes 38 to 5 minutes 12 seconds, which is the end of this video segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Don't film it. "This is for documentation. It isn't going anywhere. "What documentation? "Oh, my God. "Turn around. Let's see. Can you see through this? "He doesn't even know where he is. He is so scared and traumatised. He doesn't know where he is."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the beginning of the segment that we've just watched, we see two men in the back of the vehicle being blindfolded. Do you know who those two men are?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. That is myself and Major Janusz Kalbarczyk from Poland, and Janusz Kalbarczyk was an UN UNMO from the Sierra Echo 1 team.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you were being blindfolded, could you tell the Trial Chamber what went through your mind?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We had been told several times earlier in that day -- and, just for reference, this incident when we were blindfolded took place sometime after about 5.00 in the afternoon on the 26th of May, 1995. From the time when the armed men entered our office to when we were taken inside this ammunition storage facilities, we were threatened many times that if there would be any more bombing we would be executed and that included if there was any bombing in other areas of the country, not just around Pale. So at around 5.00 in the afternoon, our vehicle driven by a couple of Serb soldiers picked me up and also Major Janusz Kalbarczyk. I asked what was going on, where they were taking us. They didn't say anything. And then we stopped about halfway going up towards an area that Janusz was familiar with called Jahorina where there is also a ski complex, and then all of a sudden they put the blindfolds onto us. So I didn't know what the purpose of the blindfolds was, but I had -- my worst fear was that we were being taken somewhere to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the last images could you tell us who the man is who is shown next the radar structure?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The one without the weapon and the balaclava, that's Major Janusz Kalbarczyk, the Polish UNMO, and the one with the weapon in the balaclava is some Bosnian Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, finally, during the time that you were held, given what you were told, what you experienced, what did you understand was the purpose for holding you and the other UN employees?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Do you mean just on the 26th of May or for the entire time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: For the entire time.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: For the entire time, our understanding was that we were to be held in a location where they could -- that is, the Bosnian Serb military could easily move us to some locations if there was any potential bombing from NATO at the request of UNPROFOR, or if something else had occurred and they would wish to start executing us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Rechner, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you please first explain what specific tasks you had as a member of UNMO in Pale in 1995.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The specific tasks of myself was that I was the team leader and chief liaison officer of the UNMO liaison team in Pale. We were known by the radio call-sign 7 Lima, and our primary task was to facilitate communications between the UN, including the UNPROFOR forces, and the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership. We had additional functions as well. That is also to convey messages or information between the warring sides. So, for example, if the Bosnian government or Muslim forces wished to send something to the Bosnian Serb forces, it would normally go through our UN office in Sarajevo, transmit it to us, and then we would transmit that on to the Bosnian Serb leadership. And the third task we had was to assist some of the UN humanitarian agencies, specifically on the medical side, in working with Mr. Kalenic, the minister of health, and also the local hospital in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, did you have any contact with any of the officers from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Not directly. I had only met him once personally. It was in early January 1995 when there was a social function on St. Stephen's Day located in the Panorama hotel where there was also Mr. Karadzic and other Bosnian Serb leaders. So it was -- it was right after the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement had been signed, so the mood was quite positive. So on this occasion, the Bosnian Serb leadership invited my team as well as the representatives of other UN and international organisations to that celebration, so included representatives from the UN High Commissioner for Refugees based in Pale, Medecins Sans Frontiers, Doctors Without Borders, and the Internation Committee of Red Cross. But it was just a social contact. It was just -- said hello and that was about it. Otherwise I had no direct dealings with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how far the place where you were stationed at Pale was the Main Staff headquarters of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Staff headquarters, as far as we were informed, was about 60 kilometres away in a town or near a town called Han Pijesak. But we had never actually gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you speak about one aspect of your activities regarding contacts with Professor Koljevic regarding the status of UNMO observers in protected area. That's paragraph 11 of your statement. Can you please explain to the Chamber what that was actually about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I would like to have P2554, item 11, on our screens so that we can all see this portion of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Chamber what this was all about and what was your task.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. In the safe area of Zepa we had a small UN Military Observer team located there, and the Bosnian Serb military would not -- refuse them to leave for -- I can't remember now if it was for leave or for rotation purposes; that is, to exchange observers. So they're essentially stuck there. And through the Bosnian Serb military, we could not resolve the situation to get them released. Therefore, we took the initiative to contact Professor Nikola Koljevic, who was both the vice-president of the Republika Srpska government and also -- and more specifically the reason we contacted him was because he was the chairman of the Republika Srpska for co-operation with the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. Therefore, we assumed the political leadership was superior to and had some control, at least, over the Bosnian Serb military. Therefore, we contacted President Koljevic to see if at his level he could intervene to get the UNMOs in Zepa allowed to leave or rotate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, page 15, line 12 and 13, I think I heard the witness say that "Bosnian Serb military would refuse them to leave for" rather than "not refuse." That's what I heard and that's what seems to be logical in the context of the testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to clarify this through the question, but I think, Your Honour, that you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you receive any information about the reasons that prompted the Army of Republika Srpska to prevent free movement of UNMOs towards the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely in this incident what occurred. I know on certain occasions, the UNMOs were accused of smuggling in extra food to help the local population. My understanding in my discussions with those UNMOs is those accusations were absolutely false, but that's all I can say in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Following your request to Professor Koljevic, this problem was resolved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It was resolved to the point where on this one occasion the UNMOs concerned were allowed to leave [Realtime transcript read in error "believe"] Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the answer to your last question is found at the end of paragraph 11, and I noted that approximately 50 to 60 per cent of your questions trigger answers which are fully covered by the statement. So if you would please focus on any challenge to the statement rather than to repeat it -- have it repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I just noticed a slight error in the transcript at the time, line 19, 10:12:38, it is written "allowed to believe Zepa." It should state "allowed to leave Zepa," as in depart Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, within the system of the organisation of your work, who did you maintain contact specifically from the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: From UNPROFOR command, our primary contacts were our immediate headquarters. It's what we called UNMO headquarters BH command, and that was the headquarters of the head UNMO and his small staff for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As well, we had contact directly with commander of BH commander UNPROFOR, that is General Rupert Smith's office. And those are the main headquarters that we dealt with on the UN side in Sarajevo. As well, on occasion, we dealt directly with our headquarters that is the overall UNMO headquarters in Zagreb where the Chief Military Observer for the former Yugoslavia was located, as well as the staff of the Special Representative for the Secretary-General of the United Nations, who was Mr. Yasushi Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point, receive a notice that NATO aircraft was going to bomb positions of Republika Srpska prior to the 25th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We did not receive any information that bombing would be -- occurred. There was a letter that we received from General Smith where there was a threat made but nothing specific about if the bombing would occur, and, if so, what the targets would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber what did General Smith tell you in that letter with respect to the threats aimed at Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: This was not a letter addressed to the UNMOs or my office. It was a letter addressed to General Mladic. And I would need to see it. I believe it is in the court records. It was used when I testified in the case of Radovan Karadzic. But I don't want to rely on my memory to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall what the reason was for writing this letter and sending these threats by General Smith to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It was addressed not only to Republika Srpska. It was to all sides in the conflict - that is, also the Bosnian government or Muslim forces and the Bosnian Croat forces - and it was response to escalating conflict throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. So my recollection, in general, is that the letter was addressed to all sides to stop or de-escalate the conflict that was going on, particularly shelling, or else General Smith had no option but to use -- or request the support of NATO air-strikes to de-escalate the situation. But more than that, I would have to see the letter to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, on that occasion, receive any instructions relating to a possible bombing of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you personally aware of what was the direct cause for the bombing of Republika Srpska on the 25th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I am not. I was not involved in those discussions. I assumed it was based on what was contained in that letter, that the Bosnian Serb side had not complied with some of those provisions; but more than that, I was not made aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you had received information about the impending bombing of Republika Srpska or about the bombing that had already taken place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We had not received any information about bombing that would occur prior to the bombing. So when it actually did occur - we're talking about the 25th of May at about 4.00 in the afternoon - we saw two large explosions about 5 to 10 kilometres south of our location in Pale. We contacted our headquarters to find out what had happened; that is, the UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo. They also did not know what had happened, and it was only sometime after that - perhaps one hour later - that we were informed by our headquarters that, in fact, NATO air-strikes at the request of General Smith had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall if you received any official information from UNMO headquarters that air-strikes had begun at the request of General Smith?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you mean when the witness was already taken in custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I'm referring to the afternoon of the 25th, when he received first information, official information, which was at around 4.00 p.m. on the 25th of May. And we're going to further explore the question on whose request NATO carried out air-strikes, whether it was at the request of Mr. Akashi or General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, let me repeat my question: Can you recall that from the UNMO staff you received any official information at around 4.30 on the afternoon of 25th of May that NATO air-strikes were carried out at the request of General Smith?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The only information we received was either by telephone or radio from our headquarters that, in fact, those were NATO air-strikes. Whether in that communique they mentioned that General Smith ordered them or someone else, I don't recall. It was being -- it was made clear. We only assumed it was requested by General Smith based on the letter that he wrote to all sides the previous day, that is, on the 24th of May, telling them to cease the conflict activity or he would have no option but to call on NATO airpower. So I cannot answer your question precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this question has been answered, Mr. Stojanovic. Page 19, lines 14 to 15: "... perhaps one hour later - that we were informed by our headquarters that, in fact, NATO air-strikes at the request of General Smith had occurred."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now, the witness gave a slightly different answer, hence my question which I put to him again, whether this was his information or whether it was his conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are giving us a different answer from the one given on page 19, and now you said that it was your assumption that it had been done at the request of General Smith. So which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I cannot, after all these years, say precisely. I know that we assumed -- or I was led to believe at the time that it was ordered by General Smith. Whether that was just my assumption based on the letter or whether that's what had been communicated to us by our headquarters, I can now not say clearly one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in the Pale area and the broader area of Sarajevo there was a special unit of the British Army deployed there whose task was to identify the targets and to guide NATO aircraft to engage these targets?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we were not aware of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the closest UNPROFOR unit was located? And I mean the one closest to your compound in Pale.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that was contingent from the French Battalion at or near Lukavica barracks in Sarajevo, if we're talking about the UNPROFOR peacekeeping forces, not the UNMO teams. Of course, there was the other UNMO team located in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the task of this other team in Pale, UNMO team, designed or devised differently from the task that you had?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Our UNMO team was the only one in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I know, that had the liaison function as its primary and, essentially, sole role. The other UNMO teams were organised in a way that they could be near the confrontation lines and to investigate violations of the cease-fire agreement or also monitor conflict activity and report information to their sector, Sarajevo headquarters, that is not General Smith's office but subordinate headquarters which is called Sector Sarajevo, commanded, I believe, at the time by a French general, General Soubirou. So it was -- the UNMOs had the task of verifying compliance with the cease-fire agreements and also keeping the UN headquarters informed of the actual situation on the ground. And want to emphasise that everything was done in the open. They were normally accompanied by liaison officers from the respective side, military side, that they were working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a unit within their composition, a British unit, which was designated to identify the targets and guide the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, didn't I hear the same question and the same answer two minutes ago? Or did I miss something? Or is it that you are now focussing on the -- no, it's still about UNMOs. Or is the question different? Please tell us where it is different so that we -- that we know what the questions are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my last question related to the knowledge that witness had about the composition of the other UNMO team which was also deployed in Pale and who had a different call-sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you asked what the difference was and the witness didn't mention that in this respect it was any different. But...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question, your previous question was: Did you know that in the Pale area and the broader area of Sarajevo there was a special unit. That question covers also other units, not only the witness's unit. So, therefore, the question was even broader. It's just repetition. You should refrain from doing that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, after the first wave of air-strikes on the 25th of May until the morning hours of the 26th of May, did you get any information about your status or possibly a warning that you were to leave the area to be bombed? I mean information from your command.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we were not informed by our UNMO headquarters or anybody else in the UN that our status had changed and that we were to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the witness told us before that he was not informed about any bombing. So, therefore, a warning that you were to leave the area to be bombed seems to contradict what the witness told us. He only told us that once the bombing had started, he heard explosions. So, therefore, would you please be very precise in the questions you put to the witness, avoid repetition, and also listen to his answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now ask the Chamber for a break, and just clarify with -- that I asked the witness whether before the bombing he had such information, and my question just now was whether after the bombing he got any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not inviting you to enter into a debate with the Chamber on this matter. We take a break. First, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I briefly deal with the next matter in relation to Witness Turkusic. With regard to D357 MFI, the Defence considered in an informal communication dated the 28th of October at transcript pages 15810 to 15821 were the pages where the witness testified about the map, and I would like it hear - not necessarily immediately - from the parties any submissions on the admission of this document. If you can give your short comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Actually relating to a different matter, Your Honour. Since we have a moment, I would like to tender the video which was 65 ter 22648A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22648A receives number P2556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2556 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed, and try to be focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the following day, the 26th of May, a group of people came to the facility where you were put up, and you mentioned that in paragraph 21 of your statement. I would like to know the following: When you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness seems to be indicating that he is having some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not getting the English. It's B/C/S. Okay. I didn't understand anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had similar problems, as a matter of fact. Mr. Stojanovic, could you please resume. You said: "On the following day, the 26th of May, a group of people came to the facility where you were put up, and you mentioned that in paragraph 21 of your statement." And you were then about to phrase a question. Could you please phrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The persons who arrived, according to you, you weren't sure if they were soldiers as they were -- as they all were not wearing proper uniforms. Could you explain to the Chamber what exactly you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I just observed one of the three individuals in a full military field uniform. The other two individuals had military camouflage pants but just T-shirts. As I recall, one was red, and the other was yellow. When we were driving around -- or going to Pale, we would pass through some Serb positions on the way towards Lukavica barracks, and normally we saw the Serb soldiers dressed in full uniform, not in coloured T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you there, did you gain any impression as to whether these were outsiders? I mean, was it a top part of or the bottom part which made you feel that they were outsiders or that they were together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know any of the individuals expect the one whose name was Nicholas Ribic and I mentioned him in previous testimony that he is a Canadian of Serbian origin who had gone over to fight on the Bosnian Serb side. The other two individuals I don't recall having seen before, although Oli Zidlik from my team mentioned later that one of them was an individual who lived not far. So I can't really say if these were top-level or bottom-level but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I meant by top and bottom, I meant military uniform on the bottom, and non-military uniform at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. For two of the individuals, they had civilian T-shirts on top and military pants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you gain any impression as to whether they were part of the military or were -- or that they were outsider, more or less, who had joined a military person just at one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- it's impossible for me to say. My personal impression, and that's all it is, is an impression, is that they appeared to have come up from somewhere else, although Mr. Ribic I had known, although I did not know about his association with the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he was the one who was wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and also a helmet. And all three individuals were armed with Kalashnikovs, and I recall at least one of them had hand grenades as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you only see them at that occasion, or were they with you in the days following?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic was around for much of the first day but those two individuals with the civilian T-shirts, I only saw them at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Nikola Ribic, also known as Nick. Please tell the Trial Chamber about your experiences with Nikola Ribic after these events, and what was his position during the trial in Canada? Did he explain in what capacity he came to see you on that day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: He never took the witness-stand in the trial in Canada, so he never expressed what he was doing and what his intentions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand he was tried? Was he ... what was the judgement? Could you give us some further information about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He was addressed in 1999 in Germany, extradited to Canada, and then there was two trials. The first one was declared a mistrial because some additional information had come to light. So the second trial occurred in 2005 and he was found guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Guilty of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe hostage-taking was the charge. There may have been some other charges as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he was sentenced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I believe three or four years. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The other person you mention in your statement in connection with these events on the 26th of May in the morning hours is one Srdjan. Did you have the opportunity to meet a man by that name before?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Srdjan Knezevic ring a bell? Could that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No. I don't know that name. The only time that I recall having seen this individual or heard about him was on the 26th of May in the morning, when he took us from our office to the ammunition bunkers, and I don't recall seeing him on any other day after that. And I don't know what his last name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you -- sorry, just a second, Mr. Lukic [sic]. Mr. Rechner, I'm a little bit confused by your answer. At page 28, lines 9 to 11, the question to you was: "The other person you mention in your statement in connection with these events on the 26th of May in the morning hours is one Srdjan. Did you have the opportunity to meet a man by that name before?" You said, "No, I had not." Now, at line 15 when you were being asked whether the name Srdjan Knezevic rings a bell, you say you don't know that name. The only time that you recall having seen this individual -- now, or heard about him was on the 26th of May. When you say "this individual," are you referring to Srdjan or are you referring to the person you are mentioning in your statement whose name you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are one and the same. I knew only the person by his first name. I assumed that was his first name, Srdjan. I don't know what his last name was. So I don't recall knowing someone by the name of Srdjan Knezovic. Whether it is the same person, if that is in fact his last name or not, I can't answer. I don't know. I just knew -- to put it into context perhaps it's better -- when we were held in our office initially with Mr. Ribic and the other two individuals, later on, Mr. Ribic mentioned that his commander, Srdjan, would be coming, and then this individual showed up. So I'm -- I don't know if he introduced himself as Srdjan. I don't think so. I think -- I just assumed based on what Mr. Ribic told me that this individual's name was Srdjan and I don't know anything more about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rechner, can I invite you to slow down a little bit when answering the question because it's very difficult for the court reporter to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, sir, whether before that event you had any contact with Nick Ribic and his mother. Did you ever meet his mother at Pale?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No. I only met Nick or Nicholas Ribic in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on paragraph 30 of your statement. This Srdjan, is that the individual you saw in the video-clip shown by the OTP who was -- who had a crutch and used it to walk?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you conclude that he was Nick Ribic's superior?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: All I know is that Nick Ribic mentioned that his superior, Srdjan, would be coming, and then this individual arrived. He appeared very much to be in charge of the group, and Nick Ribic behaved to him in a subordinate way. So that is all I can say on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The people who were -- took you to the facilities where you spent the following hours, did -- was their impression about them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Was your impression about them that they were members of the regular army or the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, we did not know. I only knew that one of the members, that is, lieutenant-colonel who was doing the filming, he appeared to be part of the regular Bosnian Serb army based on the fact that he was wearing standard Bosnian Serb army military rank. The other individuals I wasn't sure about at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this question because in your statement you say that you could not tell whether those were regular or paramilitary units. According to you, what is the decisive factor in telling that someone is a member of the army or the police or paramilitary unit? What's the critical element?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Well, for the army and police it's quite clear. There's a specific chain of command and organisation that an individual in a unit falls under. Paramilitary organisations are much more nebulous; that is, at least the way we referred to them in Bosnia. Most of them were grouped around one or two individuals, so it was like a private armed group. Now, what the relationship between some of these paramilitary groups and the actual local police or army varied, and I can't say if they were independent or subordinate or completely subordinate, completely independent. There's a whole range there. And that's nothing that I had visibility on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you physically harassed; that is, beaten or injured by any of those persons who escorted you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and under what conditions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: When we were driven from our office to this complex where these warehouses with ammunition and the hardened ammunition bunkers were located, on arrival there, the main gate was locked so we were held up there for something like 15 or 30 minutes. During that time, a group of people had gathered and one of them broke away from the group. We were handcuffed inside the car, so he opened the door. I was -- had the misfortune of sitting next to that side of the vehicle, so I got a few punches and kicks. Then he -- the guards pulled him off. He pulled out a pistol and tried the chamber around and what we thought was to get a shot off at least one at us. The guards were able to prevent that from happening, and then later on this individual joined the group of -- I'll refer to them as soldiers that had taken us from the accommodations to the bunkers. So he showed up at the bunkers not at the time that you saw initially in the video-clip but perhaps an hour later with the group and then we saw him also several more times during our captivity dressed in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. When you saw him later at several times, was that in a position where you would consider that only military would have access? Was it in an environment where outsiders could just walk in and out or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Where we were held was under the control of the Bosnian Serb army. It was clearly a Bosnian Serb military facility both where the bunkers were located and where we were used as human shields on the first day, as well as a second facility which I referred to in my statements as the Koran barracks which was a Bosnian Serb army logistical and maintenance -- military equipment maintenance facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's where you saw him again in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, because I mentioned in some of my previously testimony, that -- referred to him as a civilian. When he attacked me he was dressed in civilian clothing, and then subsequently he changed into a military uniform and joined the rest of the soldiers that were -- that had taken to us in front of those bunkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was a strictly military environment area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as we could ascertain, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The persons who protected you on that occasion and who took away that man in civilian clothes, were they -- did they belong to the group that had come with you or did you meet them by that facility?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, those were the same soldiers that had taken us from our accommodations to that facility that I'll refer to as an ammunition storage facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you speak B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I'm very rusty now. At the time, I spoke it reasonably well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to understand what the soldiers who prevented your harassment were saying to that man in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I think they were too far away from me to be able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 03825 from the 65 ter list on our screens. 03825. While we're waiting for it to load, let me add that this is the summary of a note made of the telephone conversation between General Smith and General Mladic, which took place on a the 26th of May, 1995, at 10.00. The 26th of May. Around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if we're moving to documents, I was informed that a list of exhibits potentially to be used in cross-examination was not sent, and Madam Registrar informs me that after a reminder, it's still not received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't intend to use any new exhibits except for the ones we got from the OTP during the preparation for their direct examination. This is a document that we got from the Prosecution, and it's on their list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, nevertheless, it assists the Registry to know what numbers you are likely to use rather than to try to find out which ones from the Prosecution list you might have in the back of your mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is correct. And I believe that we will submit one in due time. I don't know where the problem lies. Could we get the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will merely ask you a couple of questions that have to do with this telephone conversation. The paragraph number is 3, but, actually, it's the second paragraph. In this conversation, which corresponds in time -- or, rather, which took place at the time you were surrounded and taken away by the persons you have mentioned. In the conversation between General Smith and General Mladic, Mr. Mladic answers to Smith that he was sorry for everything that had happened but he couldn't forgive General Smith his stupidity. General Smith was responsible for the violation of the loose cease-fire and the peace in the area. He accused General Smith of crazy and unreasonable use of NATO air strikes which had put human lives at risk. He had expected General Smith would act in accordance with UN principles for the creation of peace. What was the use of all the ultimatums which had been issued by telephone or in writing? Here's what I want to ask you: At the moments you were talking about, when you spoke to General Smith's staff on that day, and I understand that you spoke to Colonel Baxter, because General Smith was not available or unwilling to speak to you at that moment, were you told anything about there being an ultimatum issued to the RS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In that telephone conversation, I was simply acting on instructions from Mr. Ribic to put him in contact with General Smith's office. So I had no discussion about any ultimatums or anything. The phone was answered by General Smith's aide who told me that General Smith was not available, so I suggested that if Colonel Baxter, that's General Smith's Chief of Staff, I understood at the time, if he would be available, he may help. And at that point Mr. Ribic grabbed the handset from me, and I don't know what was discussed, other than Mr. Ribic making the threats that if the bombing would not stop, they would start executing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this communication between General Smith and General Mladic, General Mladic goes on to say: "Was General Smith trying to threaten him? He had expected General Smith to behave as a reasonable man and as a human being. He had never initiated provocations nor attacked the UN anywhere, but General Smith had attacked him." Here's what I want to ask you: At any point before the bombing on the 25th of May, 1995, carried out by NATO aviation, did you or the other UNMO team at Pale -- or, rather, were you or the other UNMO team at Pale exposed to any threats or harassment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: There's a lot in that question. I mean, we were -- I -- at one case we had a robbery, arm robbery, inside of our office. On another occasion, our vehicle had been stolen. In the lead-up to the 25th of May, we had come under increasing restrictions of movement. Initially we could go any time outside of Pale into Sarajevo, then we were told, perhaps ten days or so before the 25th of May, that we needed now to get permission from the Bosnian Serb military headquarters to be able to cross the confrontation line to be able to go into Sarajevo, and then it became tighter that we were not to leave Pale. And on the night of the 25th after the bombing we were told not to leave our accommodation, that we understood that we were under -- being put under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On this point, can I just ask a few questions in connection to the clip that we saw earlier before the break. You were driven off in a vehicle when you were put with blindfolds in the car. That vehicle flew an UN flag. Whose vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my team's vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was driving it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, when the blindfolds were placed on us, it was one of these -- soldiers who had taken us earlier in the day. Not the ones initially at our accommodations but the ones that came with Srdjan later on. So I don't recall specifically which one of them was driving. But it was those -- that was a group of the soldiers that were driving the vehicle and also there's additional ones that were inside the vehicle with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What finally became of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never found out. It was never returned to us when we were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we get the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, paragraph 6 -- I'll first ask you to focus on paragraph 5, however: "Mladic said that General Smith was dealing with fantasy stuff when he spoke of the heavy weapons and it was the cause of the happenings and the destruction of the population. He said General Smith had no evidence and was relying on false information from his subordinates. He accused General Smith of not being an UN man but rather part of NATO in its realisation of dark goals. He asked General Smith to behave in a reasonable manner and to cease attacks on the Serb population. He welcomed everything which undertaken towards a peace settlement, but condemned the actions thus far, which he considered a catastrophic tragedy. He urged General Smith to think of the lives in his hands." On that day, were you ever informed about the whereabouts of General Mladic? And I'm talking about the 26th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No. We had no idea where General Mladic was on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But, on that day, you had a contact -- prior to your being captured and taken away, you had a contact with the office of President Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: By telephone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, on that occasion, you spoke with Mr. Jovan Zametica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you had warned him about the situation that you were in, and you speak about this in your statement, can you just please tell us what was your impression after you had finished your conversation with Mr. Zametica about what they or he himself knew what was exactly going on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Which conversation are you referring to? There was two. There was by telephone initially just after we heard some shots outside of our building, and I saw through the back of our door that there was some armed men, I had called Jovan Zametica then. And then later in the afternoon, he came with a group of other individuals while we were handcuffed in front of those bunkers and he also spoke to me then. So I'm not sure which conversation you wish me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I said before you were arrested and taken away from your headquarter. So I'm talking about the first telephone conversation. And then I will ask you later on about what transpired in your direct contact with Mr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In that first telephone conversation, before I had actually entered our office where the armed men were located, I asked Mr. Zametica if he could send some people, meaning the police or the military, if there's a local detachment, to our accommodation to see what was going on and resolve the situation. And before I spoke with Mr. Zametica, I spoke with Mr. Karadzic's secretary, Mira, who told me that these people had apparently been sent officially. So I asked Mr. Zametica what was going on and all he said was that he heard that something like that was being organised and that we should just be as co-operative as possible with these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to finish now with item 6, which reads: "General Smith closed the conversation by expressing appreciation for Mladic's interest in peace. He reiterated the Serb side must comply with the NATO ultimatums. If they did not, the matter would be out of his hands. He urged Mladic to think deeply, to consult the leadership and to recognise the road to peace began with compliance to NATO ultimatum." What I would like to ask you is this: Had you ever been educated as an UN officer to the fact that in Bosnia it was possible to issue an ultimatum to one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Maybe it's a problem with the language, but in English "ultimatum" can mean all sorts of things. So I'm not sure what you mean by "ultimatum" in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in any putting an ultimatum of whatever kind to one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I or the UNMO organisation was not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, whether he was trained in something he never participated in, Mr. Stojanovic, seems not to be very relevant at this moment. Could I ask you, Mr. Stojanovic, the last question about the content of the telephone conversations, you listened to the answer. There were no follow-up questions. Does that mean that the answer satisfies you or ... There are no further questions arising out of that answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I am going to proceed my -- with my cross-examination, and I'm not going to deal with this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, your last question about the content of the telephone conversation is literally -- the answer is literally found in paragraph 23. So if you were eliciting that answer, then you just could have read paragraph 23 and avoid any repetition because every single detail of the answer - and apparently you have no follow-up questions - is found in paragraph 23. I again urge you to avoid repetition. Cross-examination is to challenge the testimony given in-chief or to seek support for your own case. Your last question and the answer to it does not, in any way, serve the purpose of cross-examination. Please proceed, and try to be focussed, to challenge what the testimony said, and it's now the fifth time today that I have to remind you of what you're supposed to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to focus my attention to paragraph 47 of your statement, in which you speak about the second encounter -- or, rather, the first direct contact that you had with Mr. Zametica following the telephone conversation, and this is in relation with your previous answer. You said when you addressed him, he said, Well, times have changed. Now, in the light of your previous answer, I would like to ask you how you understood and what were your feelings regarding this response that you got from Mr. Zametica in this face-to-face contact with him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I expressed to Mr. Zametica my shock at how we had been treated, and that was his answer basically: Well, times have changed. So I took it to mean that he had no respect for us and what we did as UN Military Observers for him, as far as our professional work and also in our humanitarian work with the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when NATO force was bombing one of the wars parties, did you see that as NATO siding with one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I was not in a position to make that assessment. We were not involved in any consultations regarding any air-strikes before this time. As I mentioned, it also took us by surprise because we had no prior warning, so I can't comment on, you know, what the role of NATO was. This was something agreed at a much higher level, I imagine not only General Smith but probably the Secretary-General Representative, Mr. Akashi, was probably involved as well. But that's only what I assume happened; I don't know that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this took place during the spring offensive of the BH army launched from Sarajevo that was under the control of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In my role as the chief liaison officer and team leader of the liaison team in Pale, we did not follow the events on the ground; that is, the conflict in that detail to be able to comment on that. We knew that there was an escalation of fighting going on throughout Bosnia, including the Sarajevo area, but who started it and who was responsible for it, that's not information that we had; that is, my team. Perhaps other UNMO organisations such as our headquarters in Sarajevo may have that information, but not my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your communications with the ICRC, you had a kind of argument with Mr. Bolajic regarding your status. Did you feel yourselves to be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now have 05738 in e-court. This is yet another document from the Prosecution list of exhibits, and I think it already has -- or been assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar tells us that it has not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then can we please look at item 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the second page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document issued by the Drina Corps command on the 27th of May, 1995. So it corresponds with the time that we are discussing. Pursuant to an order of the Drina Corps commander, it says: "During the capture, the transfer and the detention, treat the UN members as prisoners of war in a soldierly and correct manner. Provide them with the same food and water as the VRS members get." Now, my question is: After the 27th, the 27th of May, and after this order, in view of your statement, were you treated in line of the instructions given in this order?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't believe this order applied to us. As far as I know, the Drina Corps was responsible for Eastern Bosnia, not the Sarajevo and Pale area. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think what Mr. Stojanovic would like to know, whether you were treated in accordance with this order, although not given in relation to you, but whether you were treated like prisoners of war in a soldierly and correct manner, provide them with the same food and water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I'm not sure what they mean by POWs. We were provided food and water, but we were refused medical -- contact with medical people that we knew spoke English in Pale until the second week. We were refused contact with the ICRC until two weeks later, even though they were right in Pale. It would have been very easy to organise. We were refused contact with our next of kin, and that was paramount in our minds. And we were never told that our -- that the threats that we would be killed in case there was any NATO air strikes would not be applied. So, I mean, this is not the way you treat POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, so I cannot agree with that whole statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, a question to you. Was it also your question whether that part of the treatment where the witness was handcuffed and that he and his team members were chained to military facilities, was that included in your question, that is, to treat the UN members as prisoners of war in a soldierly and correct manner? Is that -- was that included in your question? And is it the position of the Defence that the treatment of the witness as described in his statement [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please let me please finish. Let me please finish. Whether the way in which the witness describes in the statement how they were treated, that that is in conformity with the treatment of prisoners of war in a soldierly and correct manner? Is that -- was that part of your question? And do you -- is it the position of the Defence that it was, indeed, a treatment as if they were prisoners of war treated in a soldierly and correct manner? Is that -- was that part of your question and do you -- is the position of the Defence that it was, indeed, a treatment as if they were prisoners of war treated in a soldierly and correct manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 43, line 4, exactly reflects what I wanted to ask, and it pertains to the period after the 27th, that is to say, after all these ugly events that had taken place. We still claim that everything that happened to this witness took place on the 26th and has nothing to do with the Army of Republika Srpska but, rather, with the paramilitary. Everything else, though, that happened after the 27th is related to the VRS, and that is why I put my question in that manner, and I'm going to further elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at paragraph 52 of your statement, which is P2554, and let me ask you a question with regard to this portion. You say in your statement, and I think you have it in front of you, that on your way to the Jahorina radar site, you overheard a conversation between two VRS soldiers in which one said to the other that Mladic had told them he wanted to have a number of UN people filmed at this location. I'm asking you now, in relation to these events, did you give any statements after you were released on the 18th of June and after you returned to the area where you felt safe and secure?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I was debriefed by investigators from the ICTY in Zagreb a few days after we arrived there on the 19th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you fill out certain questionnaires about the events that preceded your visit to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was specifically -- the questionnaires were on the events between the 26th -- 26th of May and 18th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that, at that time, your memory and your impressions were much fresher and more specific than they are today in the light of the time that elapsed since then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In general, yes. But, I mean, there's some problems with the questionnaire and the testimony, it was done very quickly. Also, the interview was transcribed not by me but one of the investigators, so I'm not sure if there's any errors that you wish to refer to. I can address those. But, I guess, in general terms, some of the things are just as clear to me today as they were then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in that interview and in the questionnaire mentioning your overhearing this conversation between the two soldiers in which the name of General Mladic was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I would have to see that questionnaire. I can't remember if it was one of the questions or if I mentioned this in that questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this is a good time for a break. And my suggestion is that, provided the Prosecution agrees, we give the witness 65 ter 19281 [Realtime transcript read in error "19181"], which is the -- the questionnaire, so that the witness can review it during the break, and then I can put some questions to him after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the 65 ter number again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The record says "19181."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Prosecution has no problems with it, so therefore it can be provided to the witness. We take a break. You are invited to read the questionnaire during the break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you have a copy of that questionnaire to be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have it, but in the B/C/S only. But can I provide an English translation very shortly. I believe the OTP has a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is kindly offering to print it out, which, of course, I would have expected the Defence to do. You'll be provided with the questionnaire, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you explained as the position of the Defence that everything that happened on the 26th has got nothing to do with the VRS and everything that happened after the 27th was -- that it was on the VRS -- is related to the VRS. Could I ask you what your position is in relation to the 27th itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence position relating to the 27th is that everything that had been happening had to do with the paramilitary forces until such time when he was taken over by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
