utterances.text: Just for my information, for example, in paragraph 56 of the statement, the witness describes what happened on the 27th of May when he was taken outside the building in the Koran military barracks where -- where we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... one second, please. Where the witness was advised to communicate to his headquarters that they were going to be positioned in front of the bunkers again at the same locations as the previous days. So that is within the VRS -- that is what you said falls within the VRS -- is related to the VRS. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. This event described in paragraph 56 clearly speaks about what we are saying. That is to say, that all the orders were issued by Mr. Ribic. Mr. Ribic was not a member of the VRS. The VRS had nothing to do with him. And in our Defence case, we are going to present his position and his function, as well as that of the man called Srdjan. And this is what our case is going to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, if I understand you well, it is the position of the Defence that Mr. Ribic took those actions when the witness was -- had spent the night in the Koran military barracks. Is that correctly understood as your position? But not in any way related to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. We will take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Could I meanwhile hear from the parties if they can make brief submissions on D357. I would like to hear them. If not, then we'll have to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour is here and will make those submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Harbour, yes, I didn't see you but there you are. Any -- it's a D exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As you're aware, D357 is a map of Sarajevo on which Mr. Lukic's expert has overlaid a apart of the investigation file for the Simon Bolivar school incident. And the expert also made several markings on the overlay. At transcript page 15944, in arguing for admission of this document, Mr. Lukic asserted that the witness, Mr. Turkusic, had "confirmed the angle of fire" on this document. At the time I requested the transcript pages for this assertion as this did not comport with my understanding of the witness's testimony, and I've now gone back through the witness's testimony and still do not understand him to have provided any testimony to this effect. The transcript pages that the Defence provided via e-mail to us yesterday do not appear to be related to Exhibit D357 at all, so I think there must have been a misunderstanding there. However, from my review of the transcript, the only question the witness answered about Exhibit D357 was at transcript page 15845, where he was asked: "Do you agree that this sketch is correctly laid on the map of Sarajevo." And he answered: "Yes, it is. But I think that the input is arbitrary because after so much time, and given the fact that the wall was renovated, nobody can tell that the angle of descent was really 63 degrees. What kind of measurement could have produced such a result?" And after some discussion amongst the parties, not with the witness, Mr. Lukic decided to move on from that document. So, in light of this, I maintain that since this witness had very little to say about the exhibit, it should remain marked for identification until the expert who created it can explain it further and also be subject to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. I'm hesitant to invite the Defence to -- perhaps you take your time, Mr. Stojanovic, until the next break so that we don't -- are in a position that we have to let the witness wait when dealing with other matters. Would you consider to make short oral submissions after the next break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Mr. Lukic will also take part in the discussion about that, so we'll formulate our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll see when Mr. Lukic is available. Our apologies for not paying proper attention to your -- to you re-entering the court, Mr. Rechner. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suppose that you had the chance to see the questionnaire you filled in. And let me ask you now whether, at any point, you mentioned that you heard or were able to hear the conversation between the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to have go through this slowly unless you can point me to a specific paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the question on page 2 of this document; item 8. Document 19281 - that's the 65 ter number - item 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I would like to have that on the screens. The following page in both language, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second page in B/C/S as well for -- at least if you want to focus on question 8, Mr. Stojanovic. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were asked a specific question: "At the time of your capture, did you hear any communications and/or orders relating to your capture? If so, describe the orders and who was giving them." Is it correct that you did not answer this question? We don't see anything written here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not answer that question because it was not clear to me what exactly the question was asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any case, this question is asking the question at the time of the capture not on the way to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, it was -- it's very difficult for me to answer. At the time of my capture which I interpreted the moment when the people came into our room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's the point I am making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was not clear to us who these people were or why other than the telephone conversations that I had with Mr. Karadzic's secretary and Jovan Zametica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what you say at paragraph 52 of your statement you refer to something that happened when you were on your way to Jahorina, which is long after the capture, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my -- that's why I left question 8 blank and did not comment on it at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you apparently linked paragraph 52 to question 8, and that may have caused the confusion. It's not clear, not only to my colleague but also not to me, and to -- I can now say all the members of this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and ask you in another way, because you wanted me to draw your attention to similar questions that could follow from this questionnaire. Did you, at any point, while you were filling in this questionnaire or making a statement, mention that you heard a conversation between two soldiers in the course of which General Mladic's name was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly when I -- in my amalgamated witness statement, there's a footnote to paragraph 52; footnote 77. So perhaps in that document, I mentioned that. There is -- I -- I don't know if I should be in a position of suggesting, bringing up documents, but there was also an interview conducted by these two investigators from the ICTY a couple of days after I filled out this questionnaire, and perhaps I mentioned it in that interview, but without bringing up that document, I can't tell you for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you, Witness, to focus on item 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, we should briefly go back to the previous page because that's where it begins. Scroll down, please. Now let us turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say by way of filling in this questionnaire: "Do you have any information regarding your captors (names, ranks, police, military units, persons in charge, et cetera)?" You entered: "Nikola Ribic, some sort of a paramilitary unit in Pale. Then you say: "Srdjan, commander of this paramilitary unit. "Slivo Slivic, member of paramilitary unit who beat me and attempted to shoot me." Can you see that, this text that you entered in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the people who controlled you on the 26th and 27th were members of paramilitary units at Pale. What made you say that or, rather, write that on that day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In fact, it only refers to the 26th of May, 1995, not the 27th. We -- it was not myself. It was my team-mate, Captain Oli Zidlik, who after having some discussions with Mr. Sljivo Sljivic a few days after this one, Mr. Sljivic visited us in the Koran barracks where we were then being held, that explained that he was a member of some sort of paramilitary unit. And from that information we surmised that all these individuals, that is, Srdjan and Nikola Ribic, were probably from that same paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now let me ask you about the 27th. Let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Mr. Lukic [sic], before do you that. Mr. Rechner, there is a handwriting on the left margin next to paragraph 6 with an arrow from the handwritten portion pointing to paragraph 6. Is the person mentioned there who you described as a lieutenant-colonel also part of the answer to question 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is a fourth -- and there is also a civilian reporter, Snjezan Lalovic, a fifth person that applied to question 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he is not a paramilitary. You say he is a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And he explained that he was the press information officer for the Pale military garrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also ask you about qualifying your captors as some sort of paramilitary unit in Pale and compare that with your response to question 7, small (a), where you were asked whether you were able to recognise the captors as being Bosnian Serb army or were they disguised, where you said: "Plain uniforms with standard BSA shoulder patch." That seems, to some extent, inconsistent with your answer to question 6. Could you explain why you qualified them as some sort of paramilitary unit and describing plain uniforms with standard BSA shoulder patch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We saw pretty much everybody in military uniform where the shoulder patch which is just rondel with Serbian colours in the beginning, that -- in the centre. So we saw a lot of soldiers wearing that. I cannot now say if all those individuals, five -- well, certainly not Mr. Lalovic but if all four of those had that patch or just some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But regarding some sort of paramilitary unit, we really had no idea what the status of that unit was or even if they were, in fact, paramilitary. That information is only based on discussions that Captain Oli Zidlik had with Sljivo Sljivic, so we don't know where they fell into the organisation structure where they were completely independent or subordinated somehow to the BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you describe Mr. Nikola Ribic as some sort of a paramilitary unit in Pale, where you -- I think you testified today that he was the one who was wearing a normal uniform, a regular uniform. Was it on the basis of behaviour or how they operated that it came to your mind that they would be some sort of a paramilitary unit or apparently it was not exclusively uniforms, because, otherwise, they have difficulties in understanding why you qualified Ribic as paramilitary where he was wearing a regular uniform. Could you explain a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a complicated matter. Ribic -- and perhaps we could review the video again, if that's an important issue, whether he was actually wearing the -- this rondel BSA patch or not. On -- in the radio conversation and telephone conversations that he had in our office to our own headquarters and to General Smith's office when -- demanded that the air-strikes be stopped or that we would be executed, he always referred to himself as BSA soldier. And then when Srdjan arrived, he appeared to be very much subordinate to him. So I -- whether these people were paramilitaries or not, I cannot say with certainty. It's only because what my colleague, Oli Zidlik, the conversation that he had with Sljivo Sljivic, that seemed to indicate that these people were probably some sort of a paramilitary unit, but I cannot say more on the matter. I really don't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was waiting for the interpretation to finish, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now together look at something in this document, I mean your answer to item 20. If I understand correctly, you're there being asked about what you learned in more detail. It says here that: "During your detention, did you hear any communication and/or orders relating to your detention? If yes, please describe the communications/orders and who was giving them." And you answered this question by saying: "During the ICRC visit on 8 June 1995, Mr. Bolajic, who then was president of the Bosnian Serb Exchange Commission, stated to us that we were POWs officially because we were combatants. I had a short argument with him." Could this question also encompass the conversation between the two soldiers in which General Mladic was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Because this question uses the word "detention" rather than "capture," I interpreted that question to meanwhile while we were then kept starting on the -- at the end of the day of the 26th onwards at the Koran military barracks which is where we remained. So I -- it was before -- it was after the incident of driving up to Jahorina. That's why I did not talk about these -- this question of us being filmed at the orders of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I clear that what are you talking about in this paragraph is what took place on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- well, yes, my answer is about the 8th of June. But when -- the question what I meant by detention as opposed to in question 8 which states, "time of your capture, detention," I took once the situation stabilised and we were just being held inside the military facility. I mean, there's a lot I could have added, of course, to that question. That wasn't much space, so I just mentioned that point, regarding what Bosnian Serbs considered our official status to be. As I mentioned, I disagreed with that and had an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I must ask you the following: How do you see your status on the 26th of July in the early afternoon, when you were being taken to Jahorina, or, that is, to the relay stations? Were you then a prisoner or had you been captured and, therefore, at that time, in detention, or neither one nor the other? How do you understand your status to be on that 26th of July -- excuse me, May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We considered our status to be illegally captured and illegally, of course, used as human shields and hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on the 26th, while you were being taken to Jahorina with the Polish major, were already in detention. You were a detained person at that moment.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We can argue about the definition of detention, what that encompasses. UN Military Observers are a special category of people. We are protected under the UN or the international convention on the rights and privileges of -- privileges and immunities of United Nations, and in that convention under Article 6, we are protected --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise, but that was not my question. I'm not asking this in the context of a definition of your status as this defined by the one who put together this questionnaire. My question now is: Since you're saying that the 26th -- that is, the afternoon of the 26th was not the moment of your capture, and then it was not the -- during the period of detention because that came later. My question was, rather, what you understood your status to be at that time. That's the question as put by the author of the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's the case or not, Mr. Stojanovic, is still to be seen. You're interpreting the intentions of the -- the intentions of those who drafted this questionnaire. I must say, I'm not fully understanding what the gist of this question is and what it should -- and how it would assist the Chamber. I do understand that if, in the questionnaire, a difference is made between capture and detention, that you, at that point in time, try to understand that and make a distinction. Now your question, whether he was in detention, the ordinary meaning of the word detention is that you're deprived of your liberty. Now is that what you want to know, whether the witness considered that he was deprived of his liberty? Because if it's not the ordinary meaning of the word detention, then, of course, you're asking for exactly what the witness did ask for a definition of what you understand by detention. So you used the word detention. Could you -- did you refer to deprivation of liberty or did you refer to anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Stojanovic, the question you are putting to the witness here, he has just answered a few minutes ago. The question being: What do you understand -- what -- what you did understood your status to be at that time? And the witness answered you by saying he considered himself as somebody who had been illegally arrested and deprived of his liberty. I'm paraphrasing because I can't find it immediately: We considered our status to be illegally captured and illegally, of course, used as human shields and hostages. He has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question or move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. With your leave, I would like to consult my client for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's done shortly and if it is done at such a level of volume that no one can hear it, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the previous answer. Item 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back one page, please, in English. Question number 20 -- actually, 19 (d). You say there: "How were you forced to make statements?" This was the question as put to you in the questionnaire. And you answered: "No, but during our capture on 26 May and on 27 May, I was forced to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can't see the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... does anyone have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We only can see the next word which is "to communicate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if the parties would have a copy somewhere, because this is how it was uploaded, and agree on what the text reads at the last line or the following lines, then I would invite you to read it slowly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rechner, you have a hard copy in front of you of this questionnaire. In that case, you please look at it, if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, it is the same version. What I -- I can tell -- I can tell you what I think it is. It says: "No, but during our capture on 26 May and on 27 May, I was forced to communicate under threat by radio to my headquarters." That's what I was referring to communicate. I think that's what that statement should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of this assumption, Mr. Stojanovic, you may put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These questions from paragraphs 19, 20, and 6, did they create any room in the questionnaire for you or an opportunity to mention the fact that it was General Mladic who requested you to be filmed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Nothing that would trigger that specific of a response. I mean, perhaps in question 8, I could have mentioned it but it really doesn't ask that question. Eight says: Did you hear any communications and/or orders relating to your capture, not about filming. So I was at a loss to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we please look at paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, maybe this is a good time for me to tender this document into evidence, which is 65 ter 19281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19281 receives number D391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D391 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need P2554, paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you talk about your conversation, sir, with Professor Koljevic, which lasted about 45 minutes. You say here, and I'm going to focus only and the portion that is going to create the foundation for my question, which is the following, that, on that occasion, Professor Koljevic told you - and this is in the middle of this paragraph: "In contrast, the bombing of 26th of May, 1995, were conducted before a deadline were extremely serious and endangered any future working relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and the UN. Consequently, the Bosnian Serb government would need to establish a completely new working relationship with UNPROFOR. Professor Koljevic explained that the extremely high magnitude of the crisis precipitated by the bombing warranted the response of the Bosnian Serb government to take UN peacekeepers hostage." Do you have any knowledge about what Professor Koljevic is talking about? Firstly, that the bombing of 26th of May, 1995, carried out by NATO took place before the deadline expired? Do you know which deadline he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Roughly, yes. But I cannot quote it without seeing General Smith's letter of, I believe, it was the 24th of May, where he outlined to all the parties his requirements for compliance in order to de-escalate the conflict. I'd have to see the letter. But there was two parts: One was to, I believe, stop shelling of the safe areas; and the second part of the deadline was for the next day at 12.00 noon. But without seeing the letter I can't tell you specifically what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is your knowledge exclusively based on the content of that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had no other information. It was only second-hand information contained in that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the letter is in evidence. I think it is. But could we -- or could you please verify, Mr. Stojanovic, because, if it is, then we can look at the letter and don't need to ask further questions to this witness in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This knowledge that you have about the letter and the deadline would actually confirm that Professor Koljevic was right when he said that the bombing took place before the expiry of the deadline.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: All I can say about this conversation that I had with Professor Koljevic was that he was surprised that the bombing took place before 12.00 noon. How that is related to a deadline, I cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that as from the moment when the bombing of the positions of Republika Srpska started, you became an involved party in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: As an UNMO, no, I was not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was such position ever presented to you by Professor Bolajic in the presence of representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bolajic explained that we were treated as prisoners of war because we were combatants. And I took issue with that, because we were not involved in any way in the hostilities. UNMOs, as I mentioned, are protected as UN experts on mission from arrest and detention on the convention on the privileges and immunities of United Nations personnel. So how can you consider us to be combatants? And at that point, Mr. Bolajic said, Well, this is something we can discuss later on, and left. The ICRC -- just to shed some light on this question, we asked the ICRC representatives or delegates, as they were officially called there, what our status was in their eyes, and they said not prisoners of war but persons deprived of liberty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, who was then bombing Republika Srpska at that time? Was it NATO or the United Nations? Who was striking the positions; and whose air force was it that was used to launch air-strikes on the Serb -- Bosnian Serb positions in Republika Srpska? What is your view on that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: To answer that question, I would have to know precisely what the relationship was between NATO and the United Nations, and the United Nations mission on the ground, and that was not something that we had visibility on, so I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is in evidence already. General Smith spoke about it and he explained how the bombing happened. Now, can we have in e-court 65 ter document 17701?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that document, could I ask one question in relation to paragraph 62. Did Mr. Koljevic use the expression "hostages," that you were hostages and that it was, as your statement says: "It was difficult for the hostages." Did he use that expression? It's the last part of paragraph 62: "Precipitated by the bombing warranted the response of the Bosnian Serb government to take UN peacekeepers hostage while Professor Koljevic understood that it was difficult for the hostages ..." And then he used a analogy. Did he use that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes. We spoke in English. Professor Koljevic is an expert on English literature. His English was flawless. And I know for myself I never used any other term other than being treated as a hostage. So I cannot imagine that Professor Koljevic would have used some other term, otherwise I would have mentioned it so [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's your recollection that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's the word he used in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, my recollection is that Professor Koljevic agreed when I used the term hostages in relation to the way my team and I was treated. He agreed with that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 5 in both versions, item 4, entitled: Impact of the NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is an internal memorandum as you could have seen on the cover page, issued by UNMO staff in Zagreb, which is entitled: The final report on the detention of UNMOs by the VRS. In the last bullet point, it is stated: "UNMOs stated that due to the targets selected for the air-strikes and also because of the fact that the second air-strike was carried on before the deadline of the ultimatum had expired, the Serb population and authorities perceived them as out of proportion, and as a pure retaliation on the part of UNPROFOR." My question is: This conclusion reached to the effect that certain UNMOs were the ones who reached this conclusion, would you be among those UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in drafting this report. I don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What conclusion are you talking about? Because I see that the UNMOs have given statements reflecting what -- how the Serb population and the authorities perceived the actions. It doesn't say that the UNMOs perceived it as such. So, therefore, I'm a bit lost about conclusions reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did ask the witness whether he, as an UNMO, shared the sentiment and this attitude of the Serbian population and we got an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at the previous page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you asked, Mr. Stojanovic. But if you intended to ask that, I think it's perfectly clear that the witness -- well, we could ask him -- Did you consider NATO air-strikes a pure retaliation on the -- and being out of proportion? A simple yes or no would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- for my part, no. I disagree that I had -- but I had very limited insights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you explained what this document is. Can you, at some stage before you take it off, take us to page 1. Let us see for ourselves what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Could we please look at this document in e-court that I quoted from. It is an internal memorandum issued by the UNMO staff in Zagreb, entitled as: Final reports on the detention of UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please have page 4 of this same document. It reads here, in the middle of the page, fourth paragraph from the top reads: "Several UNMOs confirmed during their interview that the guards were placed at the UNMO accommodation to protect the UNMOs from violent reactions from the local population, who were looking for revenge after the air-strikes. These measures were ordered by the local BSA commanders."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the same experience and impressions after what you had gone through?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No. This did not apply to my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able, at any time, to observe between the 28th of May and the 18th of June, when you left for Serbia by bus, that the local population rallied and called for revenge because of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No. From the 28th of May until the 18th of June, we were kept inside a military facility. We had no contact with the local population, or the outside world, for that matter. And when we were being released on the 18th, we did not see any hostile crowds along the road as we were leaving Pale for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between 28th of May and 18th of June, did you experience any unpleasantness by the people who were guarding you in the Koran military facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Question asked and answered, sir. Much earlier today the witness said yes they were denied contact with next of kin, denied contact with medical people. We're going back to the same question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, were you physically assaulted, attacked, or injured, or humiliated? Did you experience anything specific on the part of the people who were guarding you between the 28th of May and the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I -- again, the second part of your question is vague. Regarding physical assault and attack, no. But we did have many arguments with our main captor, Captain Radovan Vojvodic, and his superior about why they refused to give us access to a doctor to see the ICRC and especially to make calls home. Also, we were denied to go -- leave our -- it was a very small guard hut where we were kept after the 28th, and we were not allowed outside so it was very cramped and unpleasant, and it was only, I believe, after the sixth day in our captivity that we were finally allowed outside for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, Mr. Rechner, the last we saw you, you were handcuffed. How were you kept for the duration of your detention until you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I think the 26th events are quite clear. On the 27th, we did not discuss this yet. In the morning I was taken by a couple of guards downstairs. We were in -- at that night in a different building, a big bare block, and my vehicle was there, and I was asked to radio my headquarters and they gave me a list of locations where UNMOs were being used as human shields and that we would be in positions the same day. Later in the morning, maybe an hour or so later, we were taken by not the people on the first day, but it was the people who were holding us inside this logistics maintenance facility that we understood all to be regular BSA soldiers back to the ammunition site that had been bombed the previous day, and we were kept in a small guard hut there for the duration of the day. We were not tied or handcuffed to the bunkers. However, we saw in a back room they had a whole bunch of handcuffs ready to use, so I think we were brought back there in case there was any threat of resumption of air-strikes to be used as human shields again. And then from 28th of May until the 18th of June, we were more or less left alone with small group of guards. I mentioned already the problems that we had, such as not having access to medical care, ICRC, or contact with next of kin. But as far as that we basically passed the whole time just in that small little guard house, and later on they relaxed the rules on us going outside so we were able to just go out to get some fresh air more freely than initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at the end, can we look at a video-clip, 65 ter 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please read the number slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number slowly. 65 ter number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 225448 [as interpreted]. ERN V000-78885. And I would seek assistance from our colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I cannot make any official statement at this time. I would like to say on behalf of myself and all of my friends and colleagues because we're glad this crisis is now over. After 24 days, we're glad to be going back to our different units, and it's been a difficult time but we're all okay and glad to be going. "How are you feeling, sir? "I'd rather not comment at this time. "Where are you going to be going to? You going home or [indiscernible]. "No, I still have some time within the mission. It's up to my headquarters to decide where they will send me. "Would you like to continue work here in the Serbian side of Bosnia? "Yeah, of course, as well as any other side."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that I'm right if I say that Professor Koljevic was there with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll finish with this question: Did you recognise the man standing to his right and wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I did not know who that person was, if that's what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me then finish in a different way. Does the name Dragan Kijac ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Could I inquire with you, is this any dispute -- and I'm also looking at Ms. Bibles - is there any despite about this event, whether Professor Koljevic was there and whether a Dragan Kijac because that's the clear suggestion that he was there as well. Any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to Professor Koljevic there is no dispute. With respect to the other individual, we could not agree -- we could not stipulate to that at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For lack of knowledge or disagreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll go for lack of knowledge at the moment, Your Honour. But I think there may be some disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, Ms. Bibles, how much time would you need for the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, about 15 minutes. Over the break I will work to pare that time down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I see -- Mr. Lukic, I see that you arrived, I take it, in order to make the submissions on D357.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you an opportunity to do so. If it can be done briefly so that we do not endanger the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I can do it briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was some misunderstanding when reading the transcript because I said before you decide, he confirmed the angle of fire of this one, although today maybe he testified differently. Ms. Harbour thought that I was addressing only the transcript, what is not true. In connection of this document, we have to read the statement of this witness, specifically paragraphs 24 to 27, where he testified in his statement on this issue. And he said, in paragraph 25 that his first task was to establish the azimuth. So it was -- then we have P2017, it's an official report, where there is a sketch in which this azimuth was marked, and if you want to look at the transcript, it was discussed not with the document D357, but with another one. And in transcript, it's on pages 15829, line 5, up to transcript 15830, line 1. So to understand the testimony of this witness and our cross-examination, even in -- at this moment, before our experts are here, we think that it's necessary to have this document into evidence -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The Chamber will consider the matter. We'll first verify all the sources you have referred to, and then we will decide. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, if you wish to respond briefly, then you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my only response is that in light of the clarification from the Defence that the origin of fire he referred to didn't even pertain to the witness testimony about the exhibit in question, Exhibit D357, then truly no basis has been offered for tendering that exhibit through this witness. So our objection to admission through this witness stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, he couldn't address that in his previous testimony, of course, but he was discussing the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course, the question the Chamber will have to consider is whether the evidentiary sources you referred to whether that justifies the admission of D357. We'll consider it, and we'll decide in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you may re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we have apparently an issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rechner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just during the break I was thinking about your last question to me and my answer about whether Professor Koljevic used the term hostage. I cannot say with absolute certainty that he did. But like I mentioned, I had used it, I had described our treatment as human shields, I gave him all the details, and he never disagreed with any of that. So whether he himself used the term hostage, I cannot say with absolute certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He did not contradict your use of that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not suggest that we were simply prisoner of war or detained, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would first like to go back to a communication which you were shown on cross-examination, a communication regarding a telephone call between General Smith and the accused. That was 65 ter 03825.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to tendered that 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03825 receives number P2557, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in the absence of any objections is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see the date on this communication as the 26th of May, 1995. I would like to now show you another communication between these same two individuals on the 28th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'd ask for 65 ter 03520 to be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Looking at this front sheet of this exhibit, which reflects the date of the conversation of the 28th of May, 1995, I would like to now direct your attention to the second page, to the third paragraph. If you look into the third paragraph, down about halfway, does this paragraph appear to refer to the statements made by the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, we're still at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- second paragraph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, we need the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we look at the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the section, referring to Ratko Mladic: "He said the Serb treatment of all detained UN personnel was humane and proper, although it was true there were some located in key positions, including his headquarters, which were potential targets of NATO." Would you consider that your position on the 28th of May was in a potential NATO target?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I couldn't say that the logistics facility where we were held would have been a potential target or not, but we were very close to the ammunition warehouses and the bunkers where we were on the first two days. So we consider ourselves being held at that logistics facility to be transported quickly to any potential targets in the area of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 03520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03520 receives number P2558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2558 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would next like to turn to the area of cross-examination regarding paragraph 52 in your statement. We don't need to go to that on our screens, but this is the paragraph where you describe hearing soldiers talk about Mladic wanting -- I'm paraphrasing, but Mladic wanting people filmed at Jahorina. You were questioned about not having provided this information in the questionnaire. Do you recall testifying at ICTY in 1996?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what were you testifying -- do you recall the hearing that you testified in at that point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was on, I believe, called hearing under Rule 61, where certain individuals were asked to testify, to bring the evidence forward for the benefit of both the Tribunal and also for the benefit of member states of the United Nations to work in concert better in order to arrest some of the indicted personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, paragraph 52 in the statement refers to the Karadzic 65 ter number. It specifically refers to page 494. I can advise the Court that that is the Rule 61 hearing transcript. It is not currently -- this document is not currently on our 65 ter list. However, Ms. Stewart is prepared to display this transcript and this specific reference on the screen, and we can -- we would then ask to add this to our 65 ter list and upload it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we have a look at the transcript then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may actually be more efficient to go ahead and pull the transcript to the screen, and I could -- we could read just that small section. I rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it on the screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could actually go back to page 492, down at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now at 486.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 494 then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'll read the end of the question that you were asked: "Q. Did you hear one of the Serbian soldiers in the car say anything about Mladic? "A. Yes. We had four or five soldiers in the vehicle and they were talking amongst themselves, and one of them asked a question why we were going up to Jahorina and the other one answered that Mladic had told them that he wanted some UN people filmed there."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And that would be the end of the excerpt, Your Honour, and I don't believe we needed add that, the entire transcript, if Defence counsel would agree to that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. That is Rule 61 proceedings against Mr. Karadzic and that was, you said, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, this testimony was on the 2nd of July, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any dispute about whether this was the testimony of the witness at that time, we'd like to hear from the Defence. Otherwise, at this moment, we'll leave it, because the main issue was whether he -- when he came up with this -- with this -- with this testimony or statement, when he referred to such a conversation it -- at an earlier time. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We accept that this is part of the testimony of this witness in the Karadzic case in 1996. Our questions pertained to the part related to the questionnaire which he filled in immediately after his release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. It's -- both events are close to the -- close to 1995 or even perhaps 1995. I don't remember the date of the questionnaire, but we can consider that later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During cross-examination, you were asked whether you and the UNMO team suffered harassment or threats. As part of your description in answer to this question - and this was at transcript page 36, lines 1 through 15 - you set out limitations that had been placed on your freedom of movement prior to the 26th of May, 1995. Could you tell us who conveyed the information about your movements being limited to you at those times?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. That was from the Bosnian Serb army liaison officers in Han Pijesak that we worked with on a regular basis. There were our primary contacts with the Bosnian Serb army. And there were two individuals, in particular: Colonel Milos Djurdjic and Major Kralj [Realtime transcript read in error "Kral"]. But I don't recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How would they advise you of these limitations on your freedom?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Usually it was by telephone conversation. We had a telephone connection with them, as well as fax. So it would have been either telephone or fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, finally, Your Honours, I would ask that we bring VRS order to -- to the screens. It's been admitted as P02249.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I may just make a correction in the transcript, line 25, "Major Kral," the last name is spelled K-r-a-l-j.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When this document comes up, I'm asking you to think about the questions with respect to the 26th of May and the VRS intent in response to NATO air-strikes. I would ask you to look at -- first, the date of this order, which appears to be the 9th of February, 1994. And if you could look down now to paragraph 4 which reads: "In the event of NATO air-strikes attack (but do not kill) all foreigners in Republika Srpska, including personnel of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations, take them prisoner and hold them hostage until air-strikes are discontinued by NATO." And if we could go to the next page, please, in English: "If necessary, use blackmail and exert pressure in order to have them terminate the air-strikes." Is this order from 1994 consistent with what you experienced in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In 1995, I think it was much worse. I have -- had been made aware when I arrived in Bosnia on the 31st of December, 1994, that there had been previous occasions when NATO air-strikes had occurred, but they were different in nature. They were normally on just one target, one or two bombs, and that the Serb side had been advised in advance that they would occur. In those cases, as far as the UN Military Observers were concerned, they were simply arrested and taken to a local military facility but had not been treated as human shields or threatened to be executed, like we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions arising out of re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench also has no questions, I observed that 65 ter 5738 was not tendered. I do not know whether there's any intention to tender it. The same for 65 ter 17701. And, finally, the video used by the Defence, 65 ter 225448. None of these three are tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender all of those, all three of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including the Defence video?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence would not, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's appreciated because it's not in e-court, I do understand, at this moment. But I think the Defence played it, so if the Prosecution would assist in getting it into e-court and then to have it admitted as a D exhibit, that would be the most elegant way of dealing with it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, did you want the video to be in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Let that be a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We take them one by one. 65 ter 5738, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P2559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P; that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- I'm a bit lost, as a matter of fact, which party used the exhibit. The Defence. Would we then not -- would it not be more elegant to have a D number assigned to it. Madam Registrar, the P2559 therefore is vacated and it would be D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 392, Your Honours. Therefore, document 5738 receives number D392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 65 ter 17701.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number D393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous one, I -- let me see. Yes. D393 is admitted into evidence. Finally, the number to be reserved for the video which is not yet in e-court would be, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document video number 22544A receives number D394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D394 is reserved for this video. And once it is uploaded, it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will note -- I was going to tendered four associated exhibits, one of them, however, is now D393. So I will move on to the other three. Exhibit 10577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P2559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2559 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2560 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2561 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the bar table, following the cross-examination, I would also offer 65 ter 08989, which was an SRK order dated 27 May 1995 regarding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 65 ter 08989 receives number P2562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2562 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, finally, Your Honour, also from the bar table, an UN communication regarding a conversation between General Smith and the accused from the 24th of May, 65 ter 03516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1995, yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03516 receives number P2563, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2563 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's one document, this is D394, this is the video shown by the Defence in cross-examination. We have two different 65 ter numbers on the transcript. 225448 and 22544A. We should clarify which is the correct 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. Document used and called by the Defence was number 22544A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other one was the video used by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now we have a conflict between the Bench and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The video that was actually played in court, I believe, was 22544A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A and 8 are very similar. Madam Registrar, I think everything is clear now. Yes, it is. Then, having dealt with these housekeeping matters, Mr. Rechner, they were not very exciting for you, but I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see -- I thought we would finish a little bit sooner, but in the remaining minute or so, there are some outstanding exhibits -- associated exhibits connected with Mr. Bowen. There is no objection from the Defence as to the admission of them, so maybe it is something that could be deal with rather quickly. Mr. Jeremy is here in court to deal with that, if that pleases the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't the most simple way of dealing with it be that Mr. Jeremy puts them on a list and that Madam Registrar prepares already numbers and that just by one sentence we could admit them tomorrow, that is number so-and-so, through number so-and-so, are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I say tomorrow, of course, I mean the first day on which we are sitting, which is Thursday, not tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, then one other last brief matter. It's regarding the lexicon. On the 1st of March, 2013, the Chamber admitted that as a demonstrative exhibit. In preparing our bar table motion it occurs to the Prosecution that if there was agreement with the Defence and it was acceptable to the Chamber that the lexicon would be considered evidence in lieu of the actual tendering of the underlying documents that it would save -- possibly could save some documents. I would also note for the Chamber, in preparing this submission, in looking back at the transcript, I note that both the 65 ter number and the P number are both incorrect. So to avoid confusion I will state the correct ones now. The correct 65 ter number is 28678, and the correct P number, the Prosecution exhibit number, is P1116. They are different in the -- in the original transcript. I don't know if Mr. Lukic is able to state his views now. It is somewhat of a time-sensitive matter, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic was in charge of this witness, so I think he has more knowledge about. And he is not right now with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Ivetic could have a look at it and report if he would disagree with Mr. Groome, well, let's say by Thursday. And I can't say that from the top off my head I have any clear recollection as far as the numbers are concerned. I wanted to read out two decisions. I will have to postpone that until Thursday. We adjourn for the day, and we will resume, Thursday, the 31st of October, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
